title: Episode 4 · The West · 13 states
regionDefinition: All thirteen Census West states; eleven in GeoClick, Alaska and Hawaii in labelled supplemental Natural Earth views

supplement.attribution: Natural Earth · public domain · geographic supplemental views, not GeoClick targets

intro: Welcome to episode four. First, I clear the map. Today we learn the thirteen remaining states of the West, completing our fifty-state series.
We'll explore the Rockies, the Southwest and the Pacific coast. Then labelled supplemental maps will show Alaska and Hawaii, which GeoClick's mainland map leaves out.

states.name: Montana
states.transition: Let's start in the northern Rockies with Montana, Idaho and Wyoming, directly west of the Plains states we studied last time.
lines: Montana is the broad state along the Canadian border, west of North Dakota. Mountains dominate its west, while its eastern land opens onto the Great Plains.
Its name comes from the Spanish word for mountain. Glacier National Park, established in 1910, lies in Montana's western Rockies.
Remember Montana above Wyoming, with Idaho along its irregular western edge. Idaho is our next stop.

states.name: Idaho
lines: Idaho is the state with a narrow northern panhandle below Canada and a wider southern body. It sits between the Pacific states and Montana and Wyoming.
The card points to Hells Canyon on the Oregon border. Carved by the Snake River, it is North America's deepest river gorge.
Use Idaho's bent outline as a memory hook: a narrow top and a broader bottom. Wyoming is to the southeast.

states.name: Wyoming
lines: Wyoming is the near-rectangular state directly below Montana and above Colorado. Idaho is to its west, and the Dakotas and Nebraska are to its east.
Wyoming Territory granted women voting rights in 1869. Yellowstone, much of it in Wyoming, became the first U.S. national park in 1872.
Remember this vertical Rocky Mountain stack: Montana, Wyoming, Colorado. We now move south to Colorado and the Four Corners states.

states.name: Colorado
states.transition: Our next view holds the Four Corners group: Colorado, New Mexico, Arizona and Utah. We'll trace them clockwise around their shared meeting point.
lines: Colorado is the broad rectangle below Wyoming and west of Kansas. Utah is to its west, and New Mexico directly below it.
Its Spanish name means coloured red, referring to the Colorado River. The card's elevation fact is striking: its lowest point is higher than the highest point in eighteen other states.
Keep Colorado at the northeastern corner of our group. New Mexico is immediately south, beginning our clockwise loop.

states.name: New Mexico
lines: New Mexico lies south of Colorado and east of Arizona. Texas borders it to the east and south; a short southern stretch touches Mexico.
The card recalls Trinity: the world's first atomic bomb test took place in New Mexico in July 1945, after development work at Los Alamos.
Remember New Mexico as the southeastern state of our Four Corners group. Arizona is directly to its west.

states.name: Arizona
lines: Arizona is west of New Mexico and south of Utah. Its southern border meets Mexico, while its western edge follows the Colorado River in places.
The Grand Canyon is Arizona's memory hook. The Colorado River carved this landscape; the canyon extends about 277 miles, or 446 kilometres, along the river.
Keep Arizona below Utah and beside New Mexico. We now move north to Utah, completing the loop.

states.name: Utah
lines: Utah sits north of Arizona and west of Colorado. Notice the notch in its northeastern corner, with Wyoming beyond it.
Its name is connected with the Ute people. The Great Salt Lake is the largest natural lake west of the Mississippi, a memorable feature of northern Utah.
Our Four Corners loop is Colorado, New Mexico, Arizona, Utah. Nevada lies west of Utah and leads us toward the Pacific states.

states.name: Nevada
states.transition: Now turn west to Nevada and California. We'll follow the inland mountains to the Pacific, then travel north along the coast.
lines: Nevada lies between California and Utah, below Oregon and Idaho. Its long diagonal western border fits against California.
Its Spanish name means snow-covered, from the Sierra Nevada. Hoover Dam, on the Arizona border, was built during the 1930s.
Remember Nevada just inland from California. The angled border between them makes a useful pair of matching outlines.

states.name: California
lines: California is the long Pacific state west of Nevada. Oregon is above it, and Mexico below its southern border.
Its name comes from a fictional island ruled by Queen Calafia. The state also contains Mount Whitney and Death Valley, the highest and lowest points in the contiguous United States.
Use California's long coast and angled inland edge to remember its shape. Next, follow that coast north into Oregon.

states.name: Oregon
states.transition: Let's bring the Pacific Northwest closer. Oregon and Washington form our final mainland pair, with the ocean to the west and Idaho inland.
lines: Oregon is the Pacific state between California and Washington. Idaho is to the east, across part of the Snake River boundary.
Its name has an uncertain origin. Crater Lake, formed in the caldera of a collapsed volcano, is the deepest lake in the United States.
Remember the three-state Pacific coast chain: California, Oregon, Washington. We move north to Washington next.

states.name: Washington
lines: Washington is the northwestern corner of the contiguous states. Canada is above it, Oregon below it and Idaho to the east.
It is the only state named for a U.S. president: George Washington. Mount St Helens, also here, underwent its major landscape-changing eruption in 1980.
Keep Washington State on the Pacific, far from Washington, D.C. We've finished the eleven mainland states; Alaska and Hawaii remain.

states.name: Alaska
states.transition: GeoClick leaves out our final two states. These labelled supplemental maps show their real Pacific locations. First, Alaska in northwestern North America.
mapFacts: Alaska became the 49th U.S. state in 1959. It is the largest state by area.
The United States purchased Alaska from Russia in 1867. Alaska Native histories long predate that purchase.
lines: Alaska occupies northwestern North America, with Canada to the east and Russia across the Bering Strait to the west. Its Aleutian Islands curve into the Pacific.
The United States purchased Alaska from Russia in 1867. It became the forty-ninth state in 1959 and is the largest state by area.
Remember Alaska's southeast panhandle along Canada's coast and its island chain reaching toward Asia. Hawaii lies far to the south in the Pacific.

states.name: Hawaii
states.transition: Now travel south across the Pacific to Hawaii. We'll zoom into the main Hawaiian Islands, keeping their real island-chain geography.
mapFacts: Hawaii became the 50th U.S. state in 1959. Native Hawaiian history long predates statehood.
The island chain formed through volcanism as the Pacific Plate moved over a hotspot. The island of Hawaiʻi is at the southeastern end.
lines: Hawaii is a Pacific island state, southwest of California and far south of Alaska. These main islands form a chain, not a single landmass.
Volcanism built the chain as the Pacific Plate moved over a hotspot. The island of Hawaiʻi, often called the Big Island, is at the southeastern end.
Hawaii became the fiftieth state in 1959. Its Native Hawaiian history long predates statehood; keep the state distinct from the island named Hawaiʻi.

recap: Our mainland route covered Montana, Idaho and Wyoming; Colorado, New Mexico, Arizona and Utah; then Nevada, California, Oregon and Washington.
Across the Pacific we added Alaska and Hawaii. Those two belong in the same Western region, even though the mainland GeoClick map does not include them.
That is thirteen new states and fifty distinct states across our four episodes. Our state-by-state tour is complete. Pause, review the regional groups, and test what you remember.
